What the sea brings to the shore

by Lilliae

Summary

The waters were red. Not with the blood of a gutted fish but the hues of the setting sun sinking into the sea, yet only in one particular spot. As though there was a blaze in the depths, rising to the surface and bringing something else with it. 

Golden hair that burned red towards the ends and floated in the water all around, flickering like flames with the bob of the waves. A pale forehead. The arch of eyebrows. The dark fan of wet eyelashes.  

Two eyes bright eyes stared back.

He raised his hand in a little wave and forced a smile. “Hello. My name is Phainon. Are you a sea fairy?” 

While exploring the coasts of Aedes Elysiae, Phainon chances upon a young siren by the name of Mydeimos just before he disappears beneath the sea foam he came from.

Phainon is determined to see him again, even if it means spending every day searching the shores for a glimpse of red and gold amongst the waves.

Yet when Mydeimos finally resurfaces it isn’t with a siren song to take Phainon under with him. But golden blood dripping from a blackened wound and no one to care for him.

Notes

Saw the prompt and rubbed my devious little hands together knowing I had the perfect opportunity to write something I already wanted to write: pretty little siren Mydei.

PhaiDei week, day 6 prompt: childhood-friends

chapters.title: What the sea brings to the shore
chapters.html:
One of Phainon’s favourite pastimes was exploring the coast of Aedes Elysiae. Alone. His dad preferred fishing on the pier, his mum claimed the air curled her hair, neither of his parents liked Snowy tracking salt crystals and sea water into the house, and Cyrene didn’t like the smell and sand clinging to her for days after a single walk along the shores. 

So it was only Phainon’s footprints in the sand, washed away when the tide lapped over his bare ankles and pulled away again. He imagined monsters emerging from the waves, his sandals a shield in one hand and his wooden sword made steel in the other. 

He swung at the air, taking seashells as spoils and treasure. They would make a nice necklace for his mum or Cyrene. The pale pink ones for Cyrene to match her hair, and his mum could have a rainbow one. His would need his dad’s twine to tie them all together. 

As he bent to collect another shell, something else caught his attention. It gleamed in the sand up ahead, shinier than the stray coins that caught the sunlight just right to glint into his eyes. 

He fought against the tide splashing up his ankles and watched the water fall away from his new find. Three metal tips. A trident head attached to a polearm revealed as the sands crumbled, hauled away by the receding waves. It was forged from a red metal he had never seen before and decorated with something too pretty to be steel. 

Seawater and metal were equally cold against his fingertips as he grabbed the polearm. His arms flexed and he clenched his jaw at the sheer weight. It was heavier than that blunt sword the village blacksmith once let him hold, simply to get Phainon to stop pestering him about when he would get the real thing instead of a wooden one.  

He shifted his feet wider and braced as he bent his knees. He held his breath and pushed against the uneven ground and weighty heft of the spear. 

The head lifted free from the sand and the waves rolled in again, spilling into the empty space and lapping at the flat underside like the sea would help him force it upright. 

But the waves pulled out and ripped the spear from his hands. 

Without the counterbalance, Phainon slipped and stumbled backwards into the sand, drenched up to his chest as waves pulled in again just to mock him. His eyes stung with sea water and he sputtered out gritty salt and sand. 

The burn worsened as he blinked his eyes open, wincing against harsh daylight overhead and glittering off the sea.

He squinted. Blinked hard. Squinted harder. 

The waters were red. Not with the blood of a gutted fish but the hues of the setting sun sinking into the sea, yet only in one particular spot. As though there was a blaze in the depths, rising to the surface and bringing something else with it. 

Phainon stood and the something was too far away for him to see in detail but he could have sworn it watched him back. There was a paleness amongst the gold and red, peeking just above the surface. 

The sea roiled against him, weighing him down, encouraging him to reconsider but shoving against him when he didn’t stop wading deeper. Up to his calves, his knees, his thighs. 

The something didn’t move but the water rose over Phainon’s waist and he was finally close enough to see it in detail. 

Golden hair that burned red towards the ends and floated in the water all around, flickering like flames with the bob of the waves. A pale forehead. The arch of eyebrows. The dark fan of wet eyelashes.  

Two eyes bright eyes stared back. 

He raised his hand in a little wave and forced a smile. “Hello.” 

The something tilted their head. 

“My name is Phainon.” 

They blinked slow, pupils contacting and dilating and settling into narrowed slits. 

“Are you a sea fairy?” 

There were no similarities with Phainon’s fairy friends in the tree hollow, all cute furry creatures rather than human. But those were forest fairies and this one was obviously more accustomed to the water than the trees. Who was Phainon to judge. 

They rose out of the water, revealing a nose and mouth. When their lips parted, the sound of storms howling over waves crashed against the inside of Phainon’s skull.

“Siren,” they spoke into Phainon’s mind and then dropped back down until only their eyes remained above water. 

Phainon blinked but a smile stretched his lips. “I see. I’m a human boy.” 

They bobbed up again and Phainon knew to brace before they opened their mouth to reply in a voice like the turbulent waves that capsized fishermen, “Boy. Mydeimos.” 

At that, Phainon’s grin grew. “It’s nice to meet you.” 

Chin still above water, he nodded and his mouth opened. But no sound came. He slowly closed his mouth and his jaw clenched, brows scrunched over his narrowed eyes. 

Phainon’s brows twitched and his muscles twitched to follow the waves, stronger and faster than a moment ago as they forced him back towards shore. 

Still, he tried for another step forward as he asked, “Mydeimos, did something—“ 

Red flared on either side of his head. His lips snarled, teeth flashing. He twisted around and dove under the waves. 

Another splash of red flicked above the water in a long line that split in two at the very end and trailed with translucent red. Alongside it was the silver end of a polearm. The very same trident Phainon had failed to lift from the shoals.

The spearhead never came from beneath the waves with the same speedy precision of fishermen after a catch. Whatever blunder Phainon made to anger Mydeimos so much his whole face twisted with it, Phainon should be grateful it wasn’t enough for him to end up a bloated corpse sinking beneath the surface. 

He should be relieved that Mydeimos—inhuman in body and voice. Armed with a spear he carried like it was hollow wood while Phainon struggled like it was stone—had vanished as though he were never there. 

Yet Phainon stood in the buffering waves and winds. Waited. When no red bloomed amidst the blue by the time the sky itself tinged the seas, Phainon waded back to shore with disappointment weighing his steps.

He came back everyday. Cyrene complained about his newfound love of the coastline and Snowy whined as Phainon dropped him home after his morning exercise in the wheat fields.

But Phainon only smiled apologetically and promised to spend more time with them later. Whenever later was.

For now, Phainon spent his days roamed the shore. He always walked back to that one spot where a fire had scorched the sea only to disappear beneath its waves and was yet to resurface. When his search for that hint of red was futile, he pressed ahead. 

Some distance from Aedes Elysiae was a small cove. He had never wandered so far from home before. But the gentle waves on a peaceful day, bright yet clouded with a slight breeze to keep him cool, had guided him along the shoal until the cliffs gave way.

The shallow waters swam with fishes and he followed the curved inlet until it reached back towards the sea. It was difficult to see from a distance but there was a narrow opening in the cliff face. One that would easily be submerged during a storm but, on peaceful days like those that had passed, it was simple for Phainon to slip inside. 

He shuffled through the entrance, tucking his elbow to avoid that rock he bruised his arm on the other day, and straightened up when the low-ceiling opened up. He paused.

Long damp hair that started wheat gold and smouldered red as it flowed molten down to the dull stone. 

A rich red, vivid and glossy like the coral that occasionally washed up, honed into the three-pronged spearhead and forged into the silver of the polearm. 

The shimmering scales of a long tail half dipped into the cave’s shallow pool, flickering like firelight with every sway down to the translucent fins. 

“Mydeimos,” Phainon breathed and was echoed with the slow drip of water from the stalactites. 

But those light eyes, twins suns captured in still waters, had fixated on Phainon the moment he stumbled into the cave. His face was pale, pupils dilated and eyes hazy, lip pinned between sharp teeth. His hand tightened around his side. 

That drip Phainon thought was the condensation falling from above wasn’t water at all. It was gold, spilling from beneath Mydeimos’ hand and splattering across the ground. 

Phainon recognised it because the same thing raced through his veins with the heavy pulse of his heart as he staggered two steps forward. “You’re bleeding.” 

Mydeimos’ pupils contracted again, eyes tracking Phainon’s movements like a predator lurking behind prey. But his tail flicked and his fingers, pale webbed skin turned red towards the sharpened tips, scratched long and jagged lines into stone. Agitated. Anguished. 

The dark red fabric swathed over him and the arm pinned over the source of the blood kept Phainon from assessing the wound. The volume of blood alone prepared him for the worst. 

“Hold on,” Phainon spoke slow and moved slower towards the wall. “Let me get something.” 

Tucked underneath the shelter of a stone slab was a hidden stone box wrapped in a strip of waxed leather. Inside were a few items Phainon had accumulated over the days of venturing so far from home. 

He pushed past the twine and beginnings of a shell necklace for his mum to find a roll clean linen and a bottle of vinegar stored together in a small dish. He freed up his movements by pulling his satchel over his head and setting it aside, grabbing all three items and straightening up. Mydeimos was still staring but his trident rested untouched at his side. 

With his sharp eyes and the tilt of his head emphasising his rounded cheeks, he wasn’t so different from a kitten lurking around the houses of Aedes Elysiae. An injured stray Phainon needed to coax into trusting him. 

Phainon knelt by his side without any objections and uncorked the bottle of vinegar. Mydeimos’ nose wrinkled at the smell and he flinched away but the movement ripped a hiss from his throat barely audible over the clack of his gold and blue jewellery. 

“It’s all right,” Phainon lowered his voice into the same soothing tone his mum used when he came home with a scraped knee. “It might sting a bit but it stops the wound from getting worse. Can you show it to me?” 

Mydeimos’ mouth parted and Phainon waited for the sound of sea currents or cresting waves. But he clenched his teeth and nodded tightly. He gripped his garments and pulled it up. 

Phainon first caught on the exposed seam where Mydeimos’ scaled tail met his waist. Although the scales ended, the same vivacious red flowing up across his pale stomach in flickering lines. 

But he was confronted with the sight of brown strips wrapped tight around his torso like bandages and the sense returned to him. He wrenched his gaze away. Down to his busy hands soaking the linen in vinegar. 

The gold bled through the brown used to wrap Mydeimos’ wound, by his own hands judging by the sloppy attempt. He still couldn’t see the wound itself so he reached for his belt. 

The knife there was small. Not a weapon for attack or even self-defence. His dad gave it to him for whittling but it was just versatile enough that Phainon brought it with him whenever he ventured into the forest or along the coast. 

Mydeimos’ brows pinched but his hand didn’t move from where it exposed his vulnerable side. 

Phainon pointed at the wound dressing. Kelp, he finally realised. “I need to cut it away,” he explained and Mydeimos blinked slow at him before he nodded. Phainon swallowed. “It might feel cold. Try not to move.” 

It was bound too tight for Phainon to hook a finger in. So he pressed down on Mydeimos’ skin—cold, like plunging his hand into the pond by the courtyard during winter before it could freeze—and created an opening large enough to slide the blade in flat. 

The kelp parted and every layer that unravelled exposed just how terrible the injury was. Multiple deep gashes. Darkened flesh—blackened. Orange spindled outwards from the wounds, infecting the blue veins and glowing beneath the skin. 

What was Phainon supposed to do… 

“B-breathe,” Phainon said and took his own advice. A deep inhale, and he etched on a shaky smile but it was better than nothing. “Like that, okay?” 

Mydeimos’ face was unimpressed by Phainon’s attempt at soothing words. He breathed a quiet laugh at the flat stare and he could’ve sworn Mydeimos’ lips quirked at the very edges but Phainon didn’t waste any more time checking. He pressed the vinegar soaked linens against Mydeimos’ injuries. 

His mouth dropped open and Phainon’s eyes flitted to the thrash of water, leaping in the pool, as a low hum pressed into Phainon’s ears. It was instinct when he jerked his arm up and lodged his forearm between Mydeimos’ sharp teeth. 

The eyes that had flinched shut snapped open, confusion beneath the haze. But the low hum, pickling skin like a storm brewing on the horizon, trailed off and the waters stilled except for the ripples of Mydeimos’ tail swishing. 

Without averting his eye, Phainon shuffled into a better position. One that let him keep his hand pressed to the wound and level out the arm poised by Mydeimos’ mouth. When he was still again, Mydeimos searched Phainon’s face. 

He smiled and encouraged gently, “Bite down.” 

Sharp teeth sank into Phainon’s flesh. Phainon’s fingers twitched, clenching tighter to stage off the pain, and Mydeimos felt the muscles contract because he glanced from Phainon’s face to his hand and back again. 

“Keep going if you need,” Phainon eased out through his gritted smile. 

Mydeimos went slow and stopped without piercing too deep. Golden blood trickled from each puncture and Mydeimos’ rough, cold tongue laved apologetically. Eyes closed, face relaxed. 

Phainon hummed and lifted the linens to inspect the wound again. “That’s good. Just focus on your breathing and bite down if the pain is too much.” 

One eye opened and Mydeimos nodded, a small movement to not dislodge his teeth. Phainon grinned back, sparks of pain dissipating into bland sensation. He passed the linen through his fingers to a clean patch before pressing it to the wounds again. 

That eye winced shut. The teeth sank a little deeper and was followed by more apologetic licks. 

While Phainon cleansed Mydeimos’ wounds, he watched for signs of discomfort. Every twitch of his closed eyes was accompanied by the work of his jaw, teeth digging just a little deeper and drawing more blood to the surface that Mydeimos cleaned away before it could drip. 

Until now, Phainon had failed to notice how small Mydeimos’ face was. He had naturally narrow eyes but they still looked wide, even on his big face with its high rounded cheeks and small nose. The same childish features that made the adults coo and pinch the cheeks of Phainon and the other children his age or younger, who all squealed and ran away. 

Mydeimos was young. Bleeding and trembling, lids heavy with blood loss, hunched over in something between pained and defensive, there was little else Phainon could think of.

He didn’t know how sirens aged but, at the very least, Mydeimos looked about Phainon’s age. Maybe slightly younger. 

Too young to experience this type of pain. To be accustomed it to, based on the way he had taken the kelp and wrapped his injuries with his own hand. 

Eventually the bleeding stopped but Phainon’s simple treatment couldn’t hope to cleanse whatever corruption had seeped into Mydeimos’ body. Now that the blood had been cleaned away, the wounds looked even worse and Phainon’s carefully placed smile fall.

The pressure alleviated from his arm and he glanced up. Mydeimos’ jaw unhinged, lips and pointed teeth smeared with golden blood that Mydeimos licked clean with a flick of a tongue too long to be human. 

His face was stoic if not for the glaze to his eyes. Tears that spilled with the next blink but didn’t fall down his cheeks. Instead they collected in the smattering of scales just beneath the corners of his eyes. They shimmered, not wet but iridescent, and beaded together. 

Mydeimos leaned forward and something dropped into his awaiting hand. A pearl.

The rest came quickly, rattling where they rolled in his cupped palm. Various different sizes but all perfectly round and lustrous. Nothing like the small, misshapen pearl Phainon had once found by chance buried in the sand. 

Then Mydeimos closed his hand into a fist, crushed them all and pressed the dust against his wound. 

He grunted and Phainon heard a storm brewing on a clear day just outside the cave when he demanded, “Arm.” 

Obligingly, Phainon poised his arm ready and Mydeimos’ teeth sank in. A few deep breaths heaved against Phainon’s skin before Mydeimos pulled away again. 

When Mydeimos took his hand from his side, the crushed pearls had blackened to ash. But the skin and veins had reverted to their normal colour. 

Unsure, Phainon met his eye but Mydeimos nodded to the linen in his hand and Phainon knew what to do. He sliced off the dirtied linens so only cleans ones would wind around Mydeimos’ torso. 

His eyes were clearer now, more alert, as Phainon wrapped an arm around his waist and lowered him into the tide pool. He didn’t approve of the wound being submerged in the water but he couldn’t fathom sea water being bad for a siren. 

He sat at Mydeimos’ side, feet dipping into the water where the long tail flicked at the small fishes. Trapped during high tide and unable to escape once the tide lowered. 

“Thank you.”

Water scattered over a still sea. A quiet sound. Brief and quiet but airy and pleasant. Almost musical.

Phainon blinked at Mydeimos but his head was stubbornly fixed ahead. Even so, from the side Phainon could see where his long hair parted neatly around his ears. The fin that grew behind it, tinted red and blending into the length of his hair. The red flushing the tip of his ear was made more noticeable by the soft hue contrasted against his bright hair and fin. 

He was blushing.

Phainon whipped his head away, staring off towards the cave entrance. He rubbed his arm, prickled with pinpoint bite marks. It would probably scar. “It was no trouble.” 

Mydeimos hummed and they weren’t touching—it would be a stretch to say they were sharing air or water. Only a companionable type of close that left ample space between them—yet the sound reverberated through him. 

It sank through his skin, sifted through his muscles and eased away any tension. It thrummed through his bones. The same as settling into a hot bath after a long winter day and the warmth lifted the chill, blood sluggish and breath white, from the depths of his body.  

No wonder sailors drowned to the voices of sirens who strayed from the teachings of Phagousa. 

“What hurt you?” Phainon hurried to ask, clumsier than he should have. 

But Mydeimos was armed with a trident and a voice, equally lethal, and those injuries were unlike anything Phainon had seen before. The wounds were recent, from today, but Phainon hadn’t seen anything remotely dangerous as he traipsed the coastline without a care. 

Not to mention the warmth to Phainon’s face, melting down to his fingertips fisted in his tunic. “Are they still nearby?”

Mydeimos shook his head and his voice dropped low again, an overwhelming pressure squeezing Phainon’s chest, suffocating him, when he explained, “Black tide in the sea depths.”

Black tide? Phainon had never heard that term before. All his mind could conjure was his nights on the pier when his mind and body were too energetic to sleep, consumed by thoughts of the world outside of his village. Nights where even the moon and stars were asleep but he imagined himself out there in the wider world, living amongst stories and legends he could see playing out on the stage of the dark sea at his feet. 

It wasn’t the kind of thing that would make him tense down to the ends of his tail at the mere mention of it. That could drop the tenor in his voice until it summoned the lightless depths of the sea. That could gouge Mydeimos open and leave him for dead. 

A fish swam by Phainon’s foot and abruptly jerked away as it realised something was there when Phainon swirled it through the water. “What’s the black tide?”

That made Mydeimos’ head snap towards him. Sharp with surprise that lingered in his wide eyes and the soundless gape of his mouth. It was the wrong thing to say. 

Before Phainon could conceive of a way to rescind his words, Mydeimos twisted his upper body in a way he shouldn’t when he was still wounded. But if any golden blood was going to stain the cave until the tide next rose to wash it clean, it would be Phainon’s, Mydeimos’ outstretched arm reaching for his trident. 

The stone imprinted upon Phainon’s palms as he pushed against it, considering tentatively shuffling away. Mydeimos had a tail so, surely, if Phainon got far enough away from the water he would be able to escape. 

Although, considering Mydeimos plucked the trident up with one hand when Phainon had struggled to lift it with two, he didn’t like his odds. He could already feel the three-pronged pain lanced through him when Mydeimos inevitably launched the spear at his retreating back. 

Mydeimos’ looked at him and his quiet squeak echoed loud in the cave. He arched a brow but didn’t comment on Phainon’s wide eyes and rigid body leaning away from him, face burning as red as Mydeimos’ scales. 

Instead, he shuffled his trident between his hands. One end struck the bottom of the tide pool as he tucked the polearm into the crook of his elbow. He cradled the spearhead in his hand, finger curling over the curve where the staff split into three prongs. 

The metal was engulfed in a blue glow, swirling like water up from the tide pool. The red darkened to a purple, near black, as the water followed the curve of the trident and arched over the three prongs to bring the circle to a close. Then the water extended in narrow threads and the shape was familiar. Ignoring from the polearm, the spearhead had transformed into an instrument in Mydeimos’ hands. 

His red fingers plucked the strings of his newfound lyre and the air from Phainon’s lungs with it. 

And Phainon could seefeelhear the depths of the sea closing around him. But it wasn’t the insurmountable of the world’s water over him or the breathless ache in his lungs struggling for breath. It was strangely comfortable, like being embraced by the tides and the current and knowing they would help him reach wherever he wished to go. 

It wasn’t lightless either. The coral reefs swayed in colours plucked from rainbows in the sky and the fish swam in schools with scales more beautiful than Phainon had seen on the saltwater ones fished up by the pier. The only reason they could ever appear dull was because he had admired Mydeimos’ scales and nothing could compare. 

It was as though the seabed were illuminated in an all-encompassing daylight, different from the one that filtered from above in splintered rays of colours. It was beautiful. This was Mydeimos’ home? 

Phainon twisted around, feet kicking and water helping him like a firm hand at his back. “Mydeimos?” 

No reply. He could hear a pluck of strings and an accompanying voice but it was so distant. No matter how he twisted and turned and peered through the thinning crowds of fish and coral, he couldn’t find that brilliant red gleam. The more he searched the less he found of anything. 

The kaleidoscope of colours more vibrant than Phainon could have ever imagined was plunged into darkness. The faraway sun and its warmth vanished. The sea bed withered into something grey and lifeless, and then an utter blackness. 

It spread like ink bleeding through water that would never again be clean. Unending. Consuming everything in its path until the only thing to be found was darkness spindled through with an unnatural orange glow. 

A black tide that swept through the sea. 

At Phainon’s back, light still reached the depths even if life had long vanished. In front of him, the abyss shifted. 

Something lunged at him. Metal gleamed in the corner of his eye and a red trident soared past him from behind. 

And it all disappeared with the discordant pluck of a lyre string. 

Phainon doubled over and breathed. Panted and heaved. Air, not water. Air, not black and orange rot that could gouge him open and leave him to decay down to a lifeless corpse. Worse, into the very thing that had attacked him. 

When his heart no longer quivered and the sweat running down his face cooled, he lifted his head to meet Mydeimos’ eyes already on him. 

Phainon managed a shaky smile. “So that’s the black tide.” 

This time, there was no mistaking the upturned corner of Mydeimos’ lip. Not when he had time to study it and decide that it was definitely a smile. Whether Mydeimos was laughing with or at him was still up for debate. 

With the extent of his wounds and the pain it must cause, only given the most cursory of treatment, Phainon would take any smile. 

But Phainon’s smile wavered again. “Why are you…” He nibbled his lip and Mydeimos tilted his head. An encouragement. “Why are you fighting the black tide? Isn’t that something… adults should do?” 

Even if Phainon asked for a real sword, too young for any of the adults to take him seriously. Even if he spoke about going to Castrum Kremnos to train and explore the world outside of his sleepy, wheat farming village. Even if he dreamed of monsters and heroes recorded in epics… 

He knew he was too young for all that. He needed to wait, at least several years, to be old enough he could fend for himself in a world bigger than he could dream of. 

Mydeimos plucked his lyre again and a beautiful voice filled the cavern. 

Dark tides will taint our crystal currents, so we shall summon the sacred waves, draw the filth into the Grand Chalice, until Strife shines back against the black tide…

When the echo faded to silence, Phainon asked, “Who was that?” 

“Ocean Titan. Phagousa,” Mydeimos said, tiny waves warmed by the summer sun lapping over top his feet. “They found me drifting. Adopted me. Gave me their blessing so I would never drown again.” 

“Blessing? Again?” 

All the implications left him dizzy. Why was a child drifting alone in the sea? He drowned? How did Phagousa’a blessing scare off the Hand of Shadow? 

Mydeimos’ lip curled higher than ever as he pointed at Phainon. “Human.” And then back at himself, finger hovering over that red marking pressed against the centre of his chest as he smirked. “Human. Once.” 

So a Titan’s blessing could transform a human child into a siren. One with gills down the side of his neck and prickly fins behind his ears and up his forearms, pointed teeth and a beautiful tail.

But so very human in the shape of his face and eyes, his nose and lips, his small hands wrapped around a weapon. A child. 

“Are you going back? To face the black tide,” Phainon asked before he could think.  

Mydeimos’ smirk fell into the same stoic face, even more grave than before. He nodded. 

Phainon’s lips parted. Don’t go, he wanted to argue. To convince Mydeimos to stay far away from something so unnatural that only existed to kill. Before he could get himself killed. 

But not a word of it escaped him before Mydeimos’ eyes narrowed into a glare. The exact look he imagined Mydeimos gave those black tide creature before he drove his trident through their chests. 

Phainon swallowed down the bitterness. “Are you hungry?” 

Mydeimos blinked, eyelashes drier as they fluttered questioningly, and tilted his head. No longer a deep sea predator but a stray cat Phainon dangled some fish in front of. 

He grinned as he raced to grab his satchel from earlier and sit back down. He was slightly closer to Mydeimos’ side and his feet dipped in the tide pool occasionally brushed the tips of his swaying fins. 

From his satchel he pulled the lunch his mum had place by the front door ready for him. Since he stopped returning home in the middle of the day, she began to pack food for him to take on his adventures. 

Today was some unleavened bread and goats cheese, a few figs and a pomegranate, and a water skin of freshly pressed apple juice. 

He offered one bread loaf to Mydeimos but he simply stared, making no move to take it for himself.

“It’s food,” Phainon clarified.

Mydeimos blinked slow. Phainon took his own loaf and bit into it, chewing quickly so he could swallow because his dad always told him that whatever he had to say could wait until his mouth was no longer full. 

“See. It’s really tasty. My mum—“ 

He yelped as Mydeimos lunged and snapped his teeth around the loaf. His fingers flinched away on instinct when such sharp teeth grazed his skin, never mind that he gave Mydeimos every opportunity to snap it clean off earlier. Now, Mydeimos only tipped his head back and let the whole loaf fall into his mouth. 

The first chew was swift but the second and third slowed until his mouth was still. The wide eyed stared, brows high and cheeks puffed was no longer suspicious or baffled but… 

Phainon chuckled, feet kicking. “I told you. It’s delicious. Do you want this one too?” 

Exhilarated. Unbearably cute for it.

The way Mydeimos’ eyes dropped immediately to the loaf in Phainon’s hand meant yes. But he pursed his lips, resumed a thoughtful chew, and shook his head. He pointed at the loaf and then to Phainon’s lips. 

They split into an even wider grin before Phainon popped the rest of the loaf in his mouth, eager to get to Mydeimos’ next mouthful. He used his small knife to slice the fig and passed the first bite to Mydeimos. 

There was no hesitation when Mydeimos darted forwards and took the slice from Phainon’s fingers. His tail swished as the taste spread over his tongue. Phainon hurried to offer him another slice but he flicked his head away and pointed at Phainon. 

He laughed under his breath and took the slice for himself, barely chewing once before the knife fell again. Mydeimos accepted that slice without complaint. 

Mydeimos’ favourite was the pomegranate. His ear fins stood on end and his tail swished so hard it splashed water over the edge of the tide pool, splattering against the wall. He ate each slice so fast that the juice smeared his face. 

Only when no pomegranate slices remained did Mydeimos’ tail and ear fins droop. 

Phainon laughed and licked the juice from his fingers, getting out the last of the taste but none of the stains. “Don’t be so disappointed.” He wetted his hands in the tide pool. “Come here.”

Mydeimos leaned over and dropped his chin into Phainon’s open palms. Phainon’s smile froze and he resisted every urge to pinch Mydeimos’ cheeks while he blinked languidly up at him, the split end of his tail twitching back and forth. How could someone half fish act so much like a cat. 

A stilted laugh and Phainon ran his thumbs around the edges of Mydeimos’ mouth, gently at first and then more of a scrub as the colour stubbornly refused to lift. There were scales there too. Hard but smooth against his thumbs. Mydeimos didn’t seem to mind when the edges caught, only resting more weight against Phainon’s hands as his eyes drooped half closed.

Once most of the stains had lifted, Phainon withdrew his hands. Mydeimos’ eyes opened and his hands leapt from the water, clutching onto Phainon’s wrists to keep them in place. Before Phainon could question him, Mydeimos turned his head, mouth nuzzling against Phainon’s palm, and licked his fingers. 

Phainon held perfectly still as Mydeimos lapped up his fingers, tongue colder than the hands around Phainon’s wrists, long and flexible enough to wrap around each digit. Not out of fear that Mydeimos’ next snack would be Phainon’s fingers, teeth certainly sharp enough to crunch through flesh and bone, but simply because every thought was swept from his mind like a giant wave reclaiming everything upon the shore. 

It took embarrassingly long for Phainon to realise what Mydeimos was doing. 

His smile grew with the heat in his cheeks as Mydeimos carefully chased the lingering taste of pomegranate. “I promise I’ll bring you more tomorrow.” 

Tomorrow. 

He wanted a lot of tomorrows with Mydeimos. Although they had just met, it was impossible not to be endeared by him. Not only due to his otherworldly beauty and devastating voice but because every mannerism and every word made Phainon want to know more. 

He wanted to know his favourite song to pluck on a lyre’s strings. He wanted to know what Mydeimos’ life was like in the sea’s depths before the black tide, and further back to the life before he was blessed by Phagousa. He wanted to know the shape and sound of Mydeimos’ laugh.

He wanted to know Mydeimos was alive. 

Selfish desires. Phainon bit his lip to contain them. “If you’ll be here tomorrow.” 

Mydeimos’ voice rumbled low and Phainon thought a whisper of his own longing inside it. “Maybe. If the black tide rises then I will meet it.” 

“You’re still injured.” 

Mydeimos slapped his side. “I heal quickly.” 

Again, Phainon didn’t know enough about siren physiology to argue. To confront the black tide and stop it from devouring the seas and mounting land was an obligation for Mydeimos. A responsibility bestowed onto him by the one who had saved his life and give him that beguiling home beneath the waves. 

What could someone who had only met him today say against that. 

He pursed his lips. “If you go out to fight, doesn’t your hair get in the way?” 

Mydeimos’ brows furrowed. He pinched his hair and inspected it with a frown, as though he had never properly considered it until now. It was simply there in the hues of the sun setting fire to the sea. 

“Here. Let me,” Phainon offered, selfish hands twitching as his side at the opportunity to touch. 

Mydeimos let the hair fall and watched out the corner of his eye as Phainon shuffled about. He didn’t object, so Phainon gathered Mydeimos’ hair aside and sat at his back. He didn’t have a comb to hand so the best he could do was card his fingers through Mydeimos’ hair. 

The first time Phainon had seen Mydeimos, his hair had been slicked straight with water but now the tresses had dried rough and wavy. There were small tangles that caught on Phainon’s fingers but they unravelled so quickly they were difficult to distinguish from the salt crystals. 

Once he was satisfied, he began to separate Mydeimos’ hair into equal segments but, as he was splitting the hairs, a hint of blue came through the gold and red. 

He expected the same dark red and black garments over top an expanse of pale skin and red markings. What he found was translucent blue depths and the white knobs of a spine. 

Water. Mydeimos’ back was made of water. It bubbled with every breath bobbing his shoulders and Phainon watched them rise until they disappeared. 

At the long pause of Phainon’s hands, Mydeimos’ head began to turn.  

“S-sorry,” Phainon stammered out and he continued sectioning the hair. “I got distracted.” 

Before Cyrene decided she preferred her hair short, he used to sit and braid it while she recounted stories from her scrolls or tarot cards. Usually the braid would be unravelled not long after he tied the ribbon into place. At most he would get a stifled laugh, a pat on the head and the joy of seeing the braid left in for the rest of the day. 

So Phainon could admit he wasn’t particularly skilled at braiding hair but this was his best attempt yet. He took the twine from the stone box and tied off the bottom of the braid and swept it over Mydeimos’ shoulder for him to see for himself. 

“Done!” Phainon announced and pointedly looked away from Mydeimos’ bare back. 

While the garments had been relatively modest from the front, the back dipped low enough to expose the entire expanse of Mydeimos’ back. Perhaps sirens didn’t share human ideas of propriety. 

Similar to earlier, Mydeimos pinched the end of the braid. The twine tied together his hair and a number of small seashells scavenged by Phainon that morning. He lifted it to inspect and, without his hair as a shield, all of his reactions were open for Phainon’s eyes. 

His breath hitched and bubbled rapidly up his back. His gills down his neck and his ear fins wiggled. His skin flushed like his markings were slowly spreading across the back of his neck and up to the tips of his ears. 

“Pretty,” Mydeimos said. 

Said. Not with a voice that flattened waves and swayed the tide. Not a sound that Phainon heard inside his skull, but with his own ears. 

He spun, hands braced on the side of the tide pool, pulled himself up. He loomed over Phainon. His big eyes crinkled at the corners and his braid swaying with the slight tip of his head, tilted to bring out the small curl at the edge of his lip. 

Mydeimos dipped to rest his forehead against Phainon’s, the world shrinking down to the brightness of his eyes that could bring light to the sea depths. 

“Phainon,” he whispered. 

He smiled and murmured back, “That’s me.” There was a strand of hair hanging by Mydeimos’ face, too short to tuck into his braid, but Phainon smoothed it back behind his ear and fin. “Will I see you tomorrow, Mydeimos?” 

“Yes. If you don’t then you’ll see me the day after that. If not then the day after that,” Mydeimos gave a solemn promise. 

Phainon laughed. “You’re going to make me wait for you. How cruel.” 

“Even if you stop waiting, I’ll return,” his voice rumbled through that point of contact, settling right into the crack and crevices of Phainon’s skull as though Mydeimos belonged there. “I just hope you will be here when I come back.” 

That inhuman undertone had returned to Mydeimos’ voice, resonating through Phainon’s mind like a seashell against his ear. One he could pick up and take home with him and listen to the sound of tranquil waves whenever he missed the sea.

End Notes

I have IdeasTM for this verse nomming away at my brain like particularly energetic worms.

I actually didn’t write a fic for day 7 which means this is my last PhaiDei week entry. It was a lot of fun brainstorming and writing out the prompts, so I hope everyone who touched one of those fics had just as much fun.
